opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because I think the shift has been pretty profound, even for someone like me who spends all day thinking about the infrastructure underneath these models.

A couple of years ago, I'd have described AI assistants as a convenience: something you'd use to draft an email, summarize a document, maybe clean up some code. That's changed. Today it feels more like a thinking partner. When I'm working through a problem, whether it's a product strategy question, how we position our architecture, or even preparing for a board conversation, I'll often start by talking it through with an assistant. Not because it has the answer, but because it helps me pressure-test my own reasoning. It asks the question I didn't think to ask, or it lays out the counterargument I was conveniently ignoring.

The bigger change is frequency. I used to go to the assistant occasionally. Now it's dozens of interactions a day, many of them small. That's the part people underestimate. When AI moves from something you invoke once in a while to something woven into how you think, the economics of serving it change completely. Every one of those little interactions is an inference call. Multiply that across hundreds of millions of people, and increasingly across agents talking to other agents, and you realize the real challenge isn't training the next giant model. It's serving these models efficiently, with low latency, at a cost that makes sense.

So personally, the assistant has become part of my cognitive workflow. Professionally, that same experience reinforces why we're so focused on inference. If AI is going to be a constant companion in how people think and work, it has to be fast, it has to be affordable, and it has to be sustainable from an energy standpoint. Otherwise this beautiful experience stays limited to a few people, or a few moments in the day, instead of becoming ubiquitous.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts earlier uses like drafting emails and summarizing documents with today’s role as a thinking partner that pressure-tests reasoning and surfaces counterarguments.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the biggest shift is that assistants have moved from being a lookup tool to being a thinking partner. A few years ago I'd open one to get a quick answer or a code snippet, and then go back to doing the real work myself. Now I find I'm using them earlier in the process, at the point where I'm still forming the question.

Concretely, when I'm wrestling with a hard architecture decision at d-Matrix, I'll lay out the problem to an assistant the way I would to a colleague, and the value isn't that it hands me the answer. It's that it forces me to articulate my assumptions, and it pushes back on the ones that are weak. It'll surface a tradeoff I'd been glossing over, or point out that two constraints I listed are actually in tension. That's a very different role than autocomplete.

The second change is in breadth. Running a hardware company, I have to go deep on silicon, on software stacks, on go-to-market, on capital. No one person can be current on all of that. An assistant lets me get up to speed on an adjacent domain fast enough to ask good questions of the real experts on my team. It compresses the time between "I don't understand this" and "I can have a substantive conversation about it."

Where I'm careful is not outsourcing judgment. The assistant is great at generating options and stress-testing them. The decision about which risk we're willing to take, that's still mine, and I think it should be. The teams that get the most out of these tools treat them as a way to think more, not as a way to think less.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from lookup and code snippets to a thinking partner that challenges assumptions, but it does not identify the earlier role as helping express existing thoughts.

astra-6.text:
I think the shift is from an assistant that answers questions to one that helps you think through the questions themselves. Initially, you might use it to summarize something or draft an email. But as you get comfortable with it, you start saying, “Here’s an idea I’m working on. What am I missing? What assumptions should I challenge?”

That makes it a much more interactive part of your thinking. You can explore alternatives and get feedback while an idea is still forming. The judgment still has to be yours, but the assistant can help you arrive at a better-informed judgment, faster.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving beyond summarizing or drafting existing thoughts to challenging assumptions, exploring alternatives, and giving feedback while an idea is forming—functionally serving as a debate partner.

sol-6.1.text: I see AI assistants becoming more of a thinking partner. Instead of just asking for an answer, I can use one to explore an idea, challenge an assumption, or consider a different approach. That changes where I spend my effort: less on getting to a first draft and more on deciding whether the reasoning makes sense. But I still have to exercise judgment. An assistant can sound very convincing, so the question is whether it’s helping me think more clearly or just making it easier to accept an answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes assistants as thinking partners that can challenge assumptions, but it frames the shift as moving beyond asking for answers. It does not identify the starting role as helping the speaker express existing thoughts.
